Hm. Well the go to OSes for privacy freaks are Qubes OS (A royal pain in the arse if you ask me, but you can't get better, everything runs in a VM. Can't have a browser fingerprint if you deleted the VM that browser was in when you closed the tab), and Tails, which doesn't let you install it (just installs to stock Debian iirc), under the logic that running on a ramdisk makes data recovery impossible. Either are a fine choice for the paranoid (I for one keep a copy of tails on my keychain), but I feel they don't serve the day to day user that well, unless all you do is word processing and web browsing. For a beginner to linux, I can't recommend Mint enough, or if you like Macs, Elementary OS. Just know that the rabbit hole goes considerably deeper when you get to open source OSes. If you want to learn all about linux the hard way, look up Arch. I had a damn good install guide to hand, but it was hosted on Veuwer (is it down for good, is it just having an outage? No idea, haven't checked in a while). In case it ever shows up again, here's the dead link.. Either way, if looking to install arch, know that you will have to dedicate a day or two to the process, and should have another functional machine to hand, because if its your first time, it will take that. There is a reward for that work, however; is unprecedented control over every aspect of your machine. As soon as wine gets support for a particular application I use daily (or I have a few weeks to write the support in myself), I'll be switching to arch full time, simply because I am sick of fighting with windows 7 on things the user should have control of, like window management and taskbar behavior.

If you are looking for something in between the Baby's first linux of Mint and Elementary, but don't want to take the leap to a hobbyist OS like arch, stock Debian or Fedora are great places to be, or OpenSUSE if you use a lot of enterprise applications. And if you play games, Chapeau linux is a fork of Fedora designed for gamers, or you can go over to Ubuntu, which is still in the easy to use category like mint (mint was actually a fork of ubuntu originally), but is the go to distribution to test against for any game developer thinking "I should do a linux port, but don't run linux myself." Do note, however, that Canonical (the ubuntu devs), are kind of like the microsoft of the FOSS world. Last I checked Amazon bloatware (albeit easy to remove things, such as just a little shortcut on the titlebar to Amazon.com) came in a stock installation; kind of a turn off, if you ask me; but there are forks available. One advantage of ubuntu and close ubuntu derivatives is that, since it held the crown for most recommended linux newbie distro for many many years (still does in some circles), tutorials and getting started guides for it are everywhere, and are fairly high quality, in a manner you simply don't see with say, OpenSUSE.

Overall, though, for someone who's biggest concern is privacy, if Qubes and Tails are too limiting for you (I think they are for daily use, at least), and arch intimidates you, I would go with a stock install of Debian or Fedora, then add some basic anti tracking measures, such as getting a VPN, and setting up multiple browser environments for different uses; Fedora especially is fairly slim, so you have a very large amount of control over whats running, and, being that this is Linux, you can always get more...

Of course, there are more distros beyond this, hundreds in fact, but really, I mentioned most of the major ones (okay, I didn't touch on slackware or gentoo, sue me); if you want to explore more, distrowatch maintains a database of Linux distros, and provides a blurb on each, as well as screenshots, and attempts to track popularity through download counters.
